title: WHY DID PAUL SAY SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE BODY”?
paragraphs:
WHY DID PAUL SAY SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE MAKES TWO PEOPLE “ONE BODY”?
Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 6 is far more disturbing—and far more hopeful—than “Christians shouldn’t have sex outside marriage.” He was exposing what happens when a body that belongs to Christ is carried into an intimacy it was never created to treat as meaningless.
There are sins people confess quickly.
And then there are sins they rename.
A temper becomes “just how I am.”
Sex without covenant becomes “just two consenting adults.”
And somewhere along the way, something God designed to communicate profound bodily union gets reduced to recreation.
At least, that is what we tell ourselves.
But then the apostle Paul says something so startling that, nearly two thousand years later, it can still stop a reader cold:
“Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, ‘The two will become one flesh.’”
Paul does not say merely that prostitution is immoral.
He reaches all the way back to Genesis.
Back before sexual brokenness entered the human story.
“For the two,” Paul says, “will become one flesh.”
Why would Paul take words associated with the union of man and woman in Genesis and apply them to a man having sex with a prostitute?
Does sex automatically make two people married?
Does “one flesh” mean every sexual partner becomes your spouse?
Does this teach that people mysteriously exchange fragments of their souls?
And if someone has already crossed sexual boundaries—once, repeatedly, willingly, desperately, secretly—are they permanently attached to everyone with whom they have slept?
Because bad theology can make wounded people believe Jesus can forgive their sin but somehow cannot untangle their past.
And Paul’s message is actually much more Christ-centered than that.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:16 is striking:
“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν;”
Ē ouk oidate hoti ho kollōmenos tē pornē hen sōma estin?
“Or do you not know that the one joining himself to the prostitute is one body [with her]?”
The word that deserves attention is κολλώμενος—kollōmenos—from κολλάω, kollaō.
It carries the idea of joining, attaching, or clinging.
Then Paul explains his statement by quoting Genesis:
“Ἔσονται γάρ, φησίν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.”
“For, He says, the two will become one flesh.”
Paul is drawing from the creation language of Genesis 2:24.
This is where we need to be careful.
Paul is not saying that visiting a prostitute creates a biblical marriage covenant.

If intercourse itself automatically constituted marriage, Paul’s argument would become strangely self-defeating: he would effectively be telling the Corinthians that the sexually immoral man had become married through the very act Paul commands him to flee.
Nor does Scripture teach the popular modern idea that sexual partners literally exchange pieces of their souls that must later be retrieved through special rituals.
The Bible takes sexual union seriously enough without our needing to invent mystical mechanisms Scripture itself does not teach.
And, in some ways, more confronting.
But it cannot therefore be made meaningless.
The sexual act participates in the “one flesh” reality for which human sexuality was created, even when human beings tear the act away from the covenantal faithfulness that should surround it.
That is part of the tragedy of sexual immorality.
We attempt to make the body say something while insisting it means nothing.
Because Christianity does not teach that your body is an accessory hanging beneath your brain.
You are not a soul temporarily driving around inside disposable flesh.
And this becomes unmistakable when you read Paul’s entire argument instead of isolating one provocative verse.
Just before speaking about the prostitute, Paul says:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
Paul’s deepest question is not simply:
“How could you sleep with that person?”
The scandal is not merely that a Christian has violated a sexual rule.
The scandal is that someone united to Christ is taking a body belonging to Christ and using it as though Jesus had no claim over it.
“Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!”
“But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.”
Joined to a prostitute: one body.
Joined to the Lord: one spirit.
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you.”
This passage is not ultimately about how dirty sexually broken people are.
It is about how sacred redeemed people have become.
That is the part shame rarely tells you.
“Look what you did with your body.”
“Look what Christ paid to redeem you—body and soul.”
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.”
Paul does not lower the seriousness of sexual sin.
He raises the dignity of the sinner whom Christ has redeemed.
And maybe that is why this passage hurts.
Because some people reading this remember a hotel room.
A night you wish you could erase.
Maybe you were looking for affection.
Maybe loneliness became louder than conviction.
Maybe you knew exactly what Scripture said and did it anyway.
Maybe everybody thinks you are spiritually strong.
But there is a room inside your memory you rarely open because you are afraid of what you will find there.
Paul does not write 1 Corinthians 6 so that forgiven people will spend the rest of their lives psychologically crawling back into that room.
He writes because grace teaches us that our bodies belong somewhere better.
And Paul knew exactly what kind of church he was addressing.
Immediately before this discussion, he lists patterns of sin that included sexual immorality, adultery, greed, drunkenness and other forms of rebellion.
Then come three of the most beautiful words in the New Testament:
Not because the Corinthians had immaculate histories.
Not because their consequences necessarily vanished.
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
This is why Christianity can tell the truth about sexual sin without surrendering people to sexual shame.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin was harmless.
He saves us precisely because it was not.
At the cross, forgiveness is not God shrugging His shoulders at what destroyed us.
The cross is God taking sin so seriously that redemption cost the blood of His Son.
And taking sinners so lovingly that He willingly paid it.
Maybe you have heard people say, “Your body count defines your value.”
Maybe you have heard the opposite extreme: “Your sexual choices do not matter at all.”
And your sin is not greater than Christ.
And your history does not possess greater authority over your identity than the risen Jesus.
What you do with your body matters.
But for the person who turns to Christ, yesterday does not get the final word.
That is why “flee sexual immorality” is not merely a frightened religious command.
It is the language of rescue.
Run because you belong to Christ.
Run because your body is not cheap.
Run because grace has given you something worth protecting.
Run because freedom sometimes looks less like standing heroically in front of temptation and more like getting out of the room.
Stop negotiating with what Christ told you to flee.
Not because Jesus will love you more if you become clean enough.
But because in Christ you have been loved at a price so staggering that continuing to hand yourself back to slavery no longer makes sense.
Do not turn grace into permission.
But do not turn failure into a throne either.
Receive the forgiveness Scripture promises to those who come to God through Christ.
Some readers need to hear something else too.
If your sexual history includes something done to you without your consent, another person's sin against you is not the same as your voluntary sexual sin.
Do not carry another person's guilt as though it belonged to you.
Christ's compassion is not confused about the difference.
He sees wounds nobody else understands.
And He is not disgusted by the wounded who come to Him.
For everyone else who knows, painfully, “I chose it”...
Repentance does not require pretending you were innocent.
It requires admitting you were not—and discovering that Jesus saves guilty people.
“I could not wash myself, so Christ washed me.”
Maybe those words need to become personal today.
Secretly consuming pornography while pretending everything was fine.
Looking for intimacy in people who could never heal what was aching inside me.
Running from God while using His gifts against His purposes.
But Jesus Christ did not meet me merely to improve my behavior.
He came to make me His.
That is the center of Paul's argument.
For the modern ear, that can initially sound restrictive.
Until you realize who owns you.
Not the person who abandoned you.
Not the person who used you.
Not the accusation repeating inside your head.
If you belong to Christ, you belong to the One who was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
Not someday when you have a cleaner history.
The body that has been sinned against.
The body in which the Holy Spirit dwells.
Your faithfulness in marriage can become worship.
Your chastity while single can become worship.
Your decision to turn away from pornography tonight can become worship.
Your restored obedience can become worship.
And perhaps glorifying God with what you have also means refusing to keep life-giving truth trapped on your own screen.
If this exposed a hidden battle, comment, “Jesus, lead me into holiness.”
If shame has kept you hiding, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
If you are fighting sexual temptation and need believers to pray with you, comment, “Pray for me.”
Somebody may need proof tonight that Christians still struggle.
And somebody else may desperately need proof that Christ still restores.
We never want to imply that giving money earns God's favor or proves someone's salvation. The Gospel is a gift of grace.
But generosity can be an act of worship when it flows from a heart that wants God's truth to reach others.
Not because clicking “Share” makes you more righteous.
Not because God needs an algorithm.
But because somewhere behind another glowing screen may be a man convinced his sexual past has disqualified him forever.
A woman certain she can never become clean again.
A teenager being discipled by pornography.
A believer who fell last night and is wondering whether there is any point getting back up.
But the blood of Jesus still speaks a better word over every sinner who comes to Him.
You may have joined your body to what God told you to flee.
You may have tried to turn intimacy into anesthesia.
You may have spent years calling chains freedom.
But if you are hearing the voice of Christ calling you home, your story does not have to end where your shame says it does.
There is a new way to live.
And perhaps the sentence you will remember long after closing this article is this:
Your body may remember where you have been, but in Christ, your past does not get to decide whose you are.
